column4: The source section says the Qur'an gathers turning, face, and pleasure here: Allah sees the Prophet's face turn heavenward, grants a qibla he is pleased with, and commands him to turn his face toward the Sacred Mosque.

The source section's phrase ابتغاء وجه ربه names seeking God's face; here Allah joins the Prophet's limited responsibility for guidance to believers' spending only to seek His face, making intention and guidance meet in one instruction.

The source section's phrase ابتغاء وجه ربه is directly echoed by the feeders' «لوجه الله»; their refusal of recompense or thanks sharpens the section's account of giving without seeking a human return.

The source section's phrase ابتغاء وجه ربه is repeated in «ابتغاء وجه ربهم»; this ayah binds that aim to patience and spending in secret and openly, extending the image from direction to sustained conduct.
The source section contrasts the seeker with the denier who turns away; here Moses and Aaron warn Pharaoh of punishment for «كذب وتولى», giving that paired rejection its own stated consequence.

The source section places the turn-away person against the one who seeks God's face; here the dying person's «كذب وتولى» is the same paired rejection, while 75:31 separately says he did not affirm or pray.
The source section's paired words كذب and تولى recur in the man who denies and turns away while trying to forbid a servant's prayer; the concrete obstruction shows what refusal to heed looks like.
The source section says the sought «وجه» is God Himself; this ayah describes people who call on their Lord morning and evening «يريدون وجهه», making that orientation a settled practice.

The source section's phrase seeking the Lord's face is repeated in «يريدون وجهه»; the command to stay with these worshippers and not let one's eyes pass beyond them for worldly adornment makes the competing direction explicit.
The source section treats وجه as both the front toward which one turns and God's own self; «فأينما تولوا فثم وجه الله» makes turning and God's face meet in a concise formulation.
The source section describes وجه as direction and as God's own self; after rejecting the star, moon, and sun in 6:76-78, Abraham says «وجهت وجهي» toward the Creator, naming his chosen direction.

The source section says its root ب غ ي/B001 means seeking and that ابتغاء carries effort; here the human being labors toward his Lord and meets Him, joining exertion to the encounter the section says ends the search.

The source section illustrates ب غ ي/B001 with seeking a lost camel; after Moses and his companion lose the fish (18:61, recalled in 18:63), they say «ذلك ما كنا نبغ» and retrace their steps, a lost-creature search that leads to their intended meeting.
The source section explicitly says the sought face endures; «ويبقى وجه ربك» states that permanence, while 55:26 supplies the contrast that all on earth pass away.
The source section identifies God's face with God Himself; «كل شيء هالك إلا وجهه» makes that reading concrete by setting the enduring divine face against the perishing of everything else.

The source section ends with seeking God and becoming content; here the faces of the saved look toward their Lord, while 75:22 describes those faces as radiant, picturing the encounter behind the image.
The source section ends in رضى, contentment; the radiant faces in «وجوه يومئذ ناضرة» belong to the following ayah's people who look toward their Lord (75:23), giving that end a visible expression.

The source section's root ب غ ي/B001 means seeking, and its «وجه ربه» is God Himself; this person gives himself up «ابتغاء مرضات الله», a close parallel in which the sought divine approval governs the whole self.

The source section's root ب غ ي/B001 describes seeking toward God; even those invoked besides Him «يبتغون إلى ربهم الوسيلة» and hope for mercy while fearing punishment, locating the true direction above every intermediary.
The source section says وجه may stand for the person himself; the good-doer who «أسلم وجهه لله» offers the whole self to God, directly clarifying the phrase's force beyond bodily orientation.
The source section reads God's face as the sought Lord Himself; «أسلم وجهه لله» describes surrender to Him, and its firm-handhold image shows the stability of that orientation.
The source section's idea of turning toward God appears as «أسلمت وجهي لله»; the speaker's submission makes the face a declaration of allegiance, not merely a direction of sight.
The source section explains وجه as a direction and as the self; «أقيموا وجوهكم عند كل مسجد» joins bodily orientation at worship to sincerity of religion, making the two senses work together.
The source section develops the face as a direction and an act of turning; the command «أقم وجهك للدين حنيفا» gives that orientation a religious object and excludes divided worship.

The source section's face-direction image is repeated in «فأقم وجهك للدين حنيفا»; this ayah anchors turning toward religion in the created disposition, adding an account of why that direction fits the human being.
The source section says face can stand for the whole person; «أسلم وجهه لله وهو محسن» combines surrender of self with good action and promises its reward, making the image practical.

The source section develops turning the face as orientation toward God; this ayah marks a boundary: turning faces east or west by itself is not righteousness, which instead includes faith, giving, prayer, and keeping commitments.

The source section names و ل ي/B007 as turning away with the body or by abandoning obedience; this ayah calls bodily retreat «يوليهم يومئذ دبره» and says it incurs God's wrath, the inverse of seeking His approval.
The source section treats turning as a bodily act; the command «فلا تولوهم الأدبار» forbids turning one's back in battle, and 8:16 names the exception and the consequence of retreat.
The source section pairs a face directed toward God with turning away; this person «انقلب على وجهه» when tested, depicting a reversal of direction whose aim had never been firm.

The source section's root و ل ي/B007 includes turning away physically and ceasing to heed; here people flee uphill «ولا تلون على أحد» while the Messenger calls behind them, a sharp scene of not turning back to the caller.

The source section contrasts the face that seeks with the one turned away; «يردوكم على أعقابكم» warns that others can turn believers back on their heels and make them retreat from their chosen direction.
The source section says turning away can mean leaving attention; when remembrance of the Merciful is made alone, they «ولوا على أدبارهم نفورا», a bodily withdrawal joined to aversion from hearing.

The source section's و ل ي/B007 includes leaving listening and compliance; this command says not to turn away from Allah and His Messenger «وأنتم تسمعون», explicitly joining the bodily verb to hearing and obedience.

The source section explains turning away as refusing to listen; after the Quran is presented as good news and warning, most «فأعرض أكثرهم فهم لا يسمعون», matching that secondary sense in a preaching scene.

The source section's account of turning away includes refusing to attend to a command; this ayah describes someone reminded by the Lord's signs who «فأعرض عنها», making the object of that refusal explicit.
The source section's image includes turning away from what one is called to heed; this ayah asks who is more unjust than one reminded of the Lord's signs and then «أعرض عنها».

The source section contrasts turning away with seeking God's face; here a man «عبس وتولى» from the blind visitor seeking guidance, and 80:10 says the speaker became distracted from him, showing that turning away can be interpersonal neglect.
The source section couples denial with turning away; this man «ثم أدبر واستكبر», and 74:24 supplies the dismissive claim that the warning is only inherited magic, completing the rejection.
The source section's turning-away figure also denies; «من تولى وكفر» states that pair and leads into punishment in 88:24, while this ayah itself marks the boundary between reminder and refusal.
The source section sets seeking the Lord's face against turning away; this person «تولى عن ذكرنا» and wants only the near life, making the rival object of that turn explicit.

The source section distinguishes turning toward from turning away; this qibla passage asks «ما ولاهم عن قبلتهم» and says God guides whom He wills to a straight path, introducing the direction change expanded in 2:143-144.

The source section reads turning as bodily direction and response to a command; the qibla is made a test of who follows the Messenger, and 2:144 completes the scene with the Prophet's face and the new direction.

The source section makes face-direction an act of allegiance; this neighbor says the scriptural communities will not follow the Prophet's qibla and warns against following their desires, adding the boundary around 2:144's command.
The source section cites turning toward as one sense of و ل ي; «ولكل وجهة هو موليها» uses that direction sense and immediately commands racing toward good deeds, linking orientation to action.

The source section uses the Prophet's face turning toward the qibla as an example of positive tawallī; this ayah repeats the command for wherever he sets out and says it leaves no argument, extending 2:144's direction.

The source section develops turning the face toward a chosen direction; this ayah universalizes the qibla command to wherever believers are, completing the scene begun in 2:144 and reiterated in 2:149.

The source section's search keeps its gaze fixed on the sought one; Abraham rejects the setting star with «لا أحب الآفلين», and the next ayat carry his inquiry through moon and sun before he turns to their Creator.
The source section connects seeking God's face with guidance; Abraham says he would be among the lost without his Lord's guidance, while 6:79 states the face he finally turns toward.
The source section's image is a face directed to God rather than elsewhere; after the sun sets Abraham disavows association, and 6:79 names his turn toward the Creator.

The source section says seeking by ابتغاء requires effort; Moses says he will persist until reaching the meeting of the seas or traveling a long time, setting the strenuous search whose lost-fish turn is identified in 18:64.

The source section illustrates seeking through a lost animal; this neighbor says the fish was forgotten and took its way into the sea, supplying the loss that Moses and his companion recognize as their sought sign in 18:64.

The source section's lost-camel example turns on finding what has disappeared; here the companion recalls the fish's strange path into the sea, the clue that makes Moses identify what they were seeking in 18:64.
The source section says the search ends in meeting the sought one; this ayah names «لقاء ربه» as the hope of the one who does righteous work, giving that meeting a devotional condition.
The source section describes ابتغاء as effortful seeking; here striving for God is answered by His guidance to His ways, tying exertion to the direction found.

The source section sets two orientations against one another; this battle ayah says some wanted the world and some the Hereafter after disobeying, while 3:153 depicts the fleeing that turns from the caller.
The source section joins seeking God's face to guidance; here Allah guides those who seek His approval «سبل السلام», taking them from darkness to light and to a straight path.
The source section names ب غ ي/B001 as seeking and ر ض و/B001 as contentment; this ayah describes pilgrims «يبتغون ... رضوانا», bringing effortful seeking and divine approval into one scene.

The source section's root ب غ ي/B001 is effortful seeking and its final word يرضى names contentment; here people adopt monasticism «ابتغاء رضوان الله», but the ayah says they did not maintain it as required, distinguishing intention from fulfilled obedience.
The source section's wording seeks God's face through giving; these emigrants leave homes and wealth «يبتغون فضلا من الله ورضوانا», a concrete cost-bearing pursuit of divine approval.
The source section presents seeking God as a single direction; this ayah names those who go forth striving and «ابتغاء مرضاتي», then forbids taking as allies those who oppose that aim.

The source section names ب غ ي/B001 as seeking with effort toward God; here the same source-section root appears in seeking discord and an interpretation, a specific contrary aim that shows the sought object matters.
The source section makes the Lord the object of seeking; this ayah warns against seeking another religion, «يبتغ غير الإسلام دينا», and gives that rival orientation no acceptance.
The source section's search is for the Lord rather than a return; this ayah warns fighters against «تبتغون عرض الحياة الدنيا», exposing worldly gain as a competing object of pursuit.
The source section turns toward the Lord; these people prefer the present life, hinder others from God's path, and seek to make it crooked, a specific reversal of the straight direction.

The source section's root ب غ ي/B001 means seeking; this ayah distinguishes seeking the harvest of the Hereafter, which God increases, from seeking the world's harvest, which has no share in the Hereafter.
The source section presents the Lord as the sole object of seeking; the counterfactual «لابتغوا إلى ذي العرش سبيلا» says that even alleged rival gods would have to seek a way to the Throne's Lord.
The source section defines ر ض و/B001 as the opposite of anger; this ayah explicitly contrasts following God's approval with incurring His wrath, clarifying the stakes of the final يرضى.
The source section ends «ولسوف يرضى»; here the soul returns to its Lord «راضية مرضية», and 89:29-30 complete the welcome by admitting it among the servants and into Paradise.
The source section's final ayah promises contentment; this call to the tranquil soul introduces the return in 89:28, where it is both pleased and approved.
The source section's search ends in meeting and contentment; after the pleased soul returns in 89:28, this ayah welcomes it among God's servants, completing the reception.
The source section ends with the seeker's future رضى; following the return and welcome in 89:28-29, this ayah names entry into God's garden as the consummating reward.
The source section ends with the human seeker becoming content; «رضي الله عنهم ورضوا عنه» makes the relation reciprocal and gives its setting as gardens beneath which rivers flow.
The source section ends with يرضى, contentment; here Allah's «رضوان» is declared greater than the gardens and dwellings, showing divine approval as the highest reward.
The source section describes turning toward the Lord as the sought orientation; this command says «أنيبوا إلى ربكم وأسلموا له», making return to God a response before punishment arrives.
The source section's root ر ض و/B001 marks contentment; this ayah says Allah is pleased with the truthful and they are pleased with Him, in the judgment scene that closes the preceding account.
The source section says the sought face remains; this neighbor states «كل من عليها فان», the passing condition that 55:27 sets against the enduring face of the Lord.
The source section's example of seeking God's face through feeding appears in 76:9; this ayah identifies the recipients as poor, orphan, and captive, giving that generosity its concrete scene.

The source section says the donor expects no human return; after the words of 76:9, these givers explain that they fear a grim day from their Lord, identifying the motive behind their unstated reward.
The source section ends in the seeker's contentment; after the giving described in 76:8-10, God protects these people from that day's evil and gives them radiance and joy.
The source section describes ابتغاء as strenuous seeking and ends with رضى; this passage concludes the feeding-and-worship account by calling the reward given and the effort appreciated.

The source section contrasts the denier who turns away with the giver who seeks God; this ayah says the condemned man neither affirmed nor prayed, while 75:32 supplies the matching denial and turning away.
The source section ends with the seeker pleased; this neighboring judgment scene contrasts radiant faces looking toward the Lord in 75:22-23 with «وجوه يومئذ باسرة» expecting calamity.
The source section's search culminates in contentment; this neighbor completes the contrast begun in 75:24 by showing those faces expecting a crushing calamity.

The source section names ب غ ي/B001 as seeking and ر ض و/B001 as approval; this verse directly joins spending wealth with seeking Allah's pleasure and pictures that intention as a garden on high ground, adding a cultivated image to the section's giving.
The source section's wording ابتغاء وجه ربه is directly matched by giving to kin, poor, and traveler for those who desire Allah's face; the verse makes face-seeking a motive for concrete generosity.
The source section joins seeking God's face with giving; this verse contrasts wealth meant to multiply through usury with charity given seeking Allah's face, whose increase is with Him.

The source section says the giver expects no human recompense; this verse describes spending without following it with reminders or injury, protecting the recipient from being made indebted to the giver.

The source section rejects seeking repayment or gratitude from recipients; this verse says kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, sharpening the ethical form of giving.
The source section's giver seeks Allah's face alone; this verse warns that charity done to be seen by people and followed by reminders can be nullified, a specific reversal of that intention.
The source section says وجه can stand for the person himself; here the speaker says his prayer, worship, life, and death belong to Allah, making whole-person dedication explicit.
The source section describes seeking as effortful and ends with the seeker content; this verse speaks of one who desires the Hereafter and strives for it as a believer, whose effort is appreciated.

The source section glosses ب غ ي/B001 as seeking and says ابتغاء entails effort; this ayah states that a person has only what he strives for, making the effort itself the basis of the eventual outcome.
The source section describes exertion in seeking; following 53:39's account of striving, this ayah says the effort will be seen, adding its disclosure before recompense in 53:41.
The source section ends with the seeker's future contentment; following 53:39-40, this ayah says the effort will be repaid in full, completing the sequence from striving to outcome.

The source section names ب غ ي/B001 as seeking with effort; this verse commands seeking the Hereafter through what God gave while forbidding seeking corruption, contrasting the proper object of pursuit with a corrupt one.
The source section's face image gives a direction toward God; this verse depicts people blocking paths and seeking to make God's way crooked, a specific reversal of the straight orientation.

The source section sets the sought Lord against turning away; this verse describes people who hinder from God's path, seek to make it crooked, and disbelieve in the Hereafter, joining crooked direction to denial.
The source section says the face turns toward God Himself; this verse forbids prostration to sun or moon and directs worship to their Creator, a clear boundary between a sign and the One sought.

The source section's root ر ض و/B001 describes contentment and approval; after danger, these people follow Allah's pleasure and return with grace and no harm, showing approval as an orienting aim under pressure.

The source section ends with the seeker pleasingly content; here Allah is pleased with believers as they pledge allegiance beneath the tree, connecting divine approval to a concrete act of commitment.
The source section's root ر ض و/B001 names approval; this verse gives the early emigrants, helpers, and their faithful followers the reciprocal reward of Allah's pleasure and their pleasure in Him.

The source section's sought face means God Himself; here Allah says He is pleased with those whose faith and loyalty are firm even against opponents of God and His Messenger, tying approval to allegiance.
The source section quotes those who patiently seek their Lord's face in 13:22; this next ayah names the Gardens of Eden they enter with their righteous kin, continuing that seekers' promised outcome.
The source section links patience with seeking the Lord's face in 13:22; here the angels greet the entrants with peace because of their patience, completing the neighboring account's reward.
The source section says turning away can mean abandoning heed and obedience; this verse describes the one who turns away from remembrance of his Lord and the punishment that follows.

The source section locates the dying denier's conduct in the moment when life reaches the collarbones; this ayah supplies that threshold scene before 75:31-32 name his failure to affirm and his turning away.

The source section says the search ends in meeting the sought Lord; this adjacent death passage says that on that day the drive is to the Lord, giving the dying scene in 75:26 and 75:31-32 its destination.

The source section directs the seeker toward the Lord and says His face remains; this ayah states the contrary preference for the near life, while 87:17 says the Hereafter is better and more enduring.
The source section says the sought face endures; this neighboring ayah calls the Hereafter better and more lasting, completing the contrast with preference for the near life in 87:16.

The source section's root و ل ي/B007 includes turning away by ceasing to heed; this ayah distinguishes people who merely say they hear from those who actually hear, following the command not to turn away while listening in 8:20.

The source section describes turning away as failure to heed and comply; after 8:20-21 warns against that refusal, this ayah commands believers to respond when Allah and the Messenger call them to what gives life.

The source section explains turning away as either bodily withdrawal or abandoning attention; this ayah depicts a person who turns away arrogantly from recited signs as if he had not heard, the secondary sense made visible.
The source section describes turning away by refusing to listen or comply; this ayah depicts someone who hears God's signs, then persists arrogantly as if he had not heard, and warns of punishment.

The source section connects turning away with leaving attentive listening; here disbelievers tell one another not to listen to the Quran and to make noise over it, an explicit effort to block hearing.

The source section joins the Prophet's limited responsibility for guidance to people who turn away; this ayah says if they turn away, his duty is only clear delivery, repeating that limit in the context of refusal.

The source section describes the turn-away person alongside a caller to heed; this ayah tells the Messenger to remind, and 88:22-23 clarify that he cannot control people who then turn away and disbelieve.
The source section says guidance is not the Prophet's responsibility; this ayah states he is not set over people as a controller, immediately before 88:23 names those who turn away and disbelieve.
The source section pairs denial with turning away and develops an animal image for the denier; this ayah asks why people turn away from the reminder, before 74:50-51 compare them to fleeing donkeys.

The source section's dictionary sense for ك ذ ب/B007 describes a wild animal running and looking back; this ayah compares people turning from the reminder to alarmed donkeys, a specific fleeing-animal parallel, though it does not show the source's backward glance.

The source section's dictionary sense for ك ذ ب/B007 uses a wild animal running before it stops to look back; this ayah says the donkeys flee from a lion, echoing flight from a threat but not the pause or backward look.
